name: Vedapureeswarar Temple, Thiruverkadu
deity: Shiva as Vedapureeswarar (Vedapuriswarar), with the goddess Balambigai
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Thondai country near Chennai, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); structural temple with later additions, reconstructed in 1973
dynasty: Early Chola patronage (attributed) and later renovators
summary: Vedapureeswarar at Thiruverkadu is the ancient Shiva temple of a sacred grove west of Chennai, sung in the Tevaram, where the four Vedas are said to have worshipped as trees and where the sage Agastya was granted a vision of the wedding of Shiva and Parvati.

sections.history: Thiruverkadu stands in the western reaches of Chennai, in the old Thondai country, and its Vedapureeswarar temple is among the ancient Shiva shrines of the region. The town is praised in the Tevaram, the seventh-century hymns of the Tamil saints, with decads sung here by Tirugnana Sambandar and by Appar, and it is on that account counted a Paadal Petra Sthalam. The name Thiruverkadu is read as the sacred grove, and the deity's name Vedapureeswarar as the Lord of the city of the Vedas, for the four Vedas are said to have come to this very place to worship. Tradition attributes the early structural temple to Chola patrons, and it was rebuilt in 1973; it is kept in daily worship under the Tamil Nadu temple administration. The town is widely known today for its Karumariamman temple, but the Vedapureeswarar shrine is the older sanctuary and the one the saints sang.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east beneath a tall rajagopuram and opens through three corridors toward the sanctum, where Vedapureeswarar is worshipped as the Shiva linga beneath an apsidal Gajaprishta vimana, a tower shaped like the curve of an elephant's back. The goddess Balambigai is honoured in her own shrine within the enclosure. Behind the sanctum stands the image for which devotees come with special feeling, a sculpture of Shiva and Parvati in their wedding form, the Tirumana Kolam, recalling the vision granted to the sage Agastya. The temple tank, the Veda Theertham, and the Velvela tree held as the temple's sacred tree complete a compact enclosure of roughly two acres, kept in careful order within a busy suburb.
sections.legends: Two stories give the temple its name and its heart. In the first, when Shiva was to wed Parvati in the Himalayas the whole world drew northward to witness it, and the sage Agastya was sent south so that the earth should keep its balance; thus he could not see the marriage he longed to behold. He prayed to Shiva at Thiruverkadu, and the Lord, moved by his devotion, appeared before him with Parvati in their wedding form, so that the sage beheld the very event he had missed. The sculpture of the divine couple as bride and groom behind the sanctum keeps this grace alive. In the second, the four Vedas themselves are said to have taken the form of trees and grown as a grove at this place to worship Shiva, and from that sacred grove the town takes its name and the Lord his title as the master of the Vedas' own city.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps four festivals through the year, of which the chief is the Brahmotsavam in the Tamil month of Magam, in February or March, when the deities are drawn in procession and the town gathers in devotion. Maha Shivaratri is observed through the night, and the monthly Pradosham, sacred to Shiva, is kept with special care. As the wedding of Shiva and Parvati is central to the temple's story, the Tirukalyanam is held with particular feeling. Dates follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm them locally.
sections.experience: Thiruverkadu rewards a quiet, attentive visit amid the bustle of a growing suburb. Enter beneath the eastern gopuram, come through the corridors to the sanctum of Vedapureeswarar, and then seek out the sculpture of the wedding form behind it, where the story of Agastya's vision feels close at hand. Devotees praying for marriage and for harmony in the home hold this image especially dear. Turn next to the goddess Balambigai in her own shrine, and pause by the Veda Theertham and the old temple tree before leaving. Many who come to the famous Karumariamman temple nearby also step into this older sanctuary to begin with Shiva.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning from around 6 a.m. until midday, and again from late afternoon into the evening until about 8 p.m.; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Thiruverkadu lies in the western suburbs of Chennai, in Tiruvallur district, about 18 to 20 km from the city centre and well served by frequent Chennai suburban buses. The nearest railheads are at Avadi and Ambattur, and Chennai International Airport is around 25 km away. The temple stands near the centre of the town, a short walk from the main bus stop.
